This supplement gives the formal definitions, parametrizations and derivations supporting the main lecture. Its details are intended for supplementary study alongside the corresponding lecture topics. For the chord calculations, $R$ is the fixed circle radius, $T$ the normalized midpoint distance, and $L$ the chord length, as in the Bertrand deck. The Billing indicator in the main notes remains $X_B$. All application records in this supplement are hypothetical teaching examples.

For the sigma-algebra discussion, follow the [two-LED experiment](#sensor-sigma-algebra), [unit-interval model](#unit-interval-triplet), [generated sigma-algebras](#generated-sigma-algebra), and [Vitali construction](#vitali-set).

The main lecture motivates these constructions with questions about a hypothetical six-ticket
routing audit, before introducing the triplet and axioms through finite calculations. The proofs below do not depend on that application; they
state the general hypotheses needed for the results.

Reference: Krishna Jagannathan, [*Probability Foundations for Electrical Engineers*](https://www.ee.iitm.ac.in/~krishnaj/ee5110notes.htm), 9 July 2025, Chapters 1, 4 and 11, particularly Definitions 68–70 for measurable functions, random variables and their laws. The calculations of the sampling maps are written out below.

## 1. Outcomes, events and mutual exclusivity

A sample space is required to satisfy two conditions. It must be **exhaustive**, so that at least one of its elements occurs in any realization of the experiment, and its elements must be **mutually exclusive**, so that at most one of them occurs. Together these state that exactly one $\omega\in\Omega$ occurs each time the experiment is performed.

Distinct outcomes correspond to disjoint singleton subsets. When these
singletons belong to the event collection, they are singleton events:

$$\{\omega_1\}\cap\{\omega_2\}=\varnothing\quad\text{whenever }\omega_1\ne\omega_2 .$$

For countable $\Omega$ the singletons therefore form a countable disjoint partition, $\Omega=\bigcup_{\omega\in\Omega}\{\omega\}$ (a disjoint union).

**Outcomes are mutually exclusive; events need not be.** For a single roll of a die, $\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, and the outcomes $2$ and $4$ cannot both occur. The events

$$A=\{2,4,6\}\ \text{(even)},\qquad B=\{4,5,6\}\ \text{(greater than 3)}$$

can both occur, since $A\cap B=\{4,6\}\ne\varnothing$.

### Consequences for calculation

The two cases are handled by different rules, and the distinction above is what separates them.

Because singletons are disjoint, countable additivity applies directly to them, and for a countable event $A$ whose singletons are measurable

$$P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}P(\{\omega\}).$$

For two events no such rule is available, since additivity requires disjointness. The correction term is the shared part:

$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).$$

Writing $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$ for the die events above would count the outcomes $4$ and $6$ twice.

### Two errors that this distinction prevents

**A list of events is not a sample space.** For one roll of a die, the pair “even” and “greater than 3” is not a sample space: both can occur in a single roll, so the second condition fails. They are events in the finer space $\{1,\ldots,6\}$.

**A valid sample space need not have equally likely elements.** For two independent fair tosses, the list “a head on the first toss”, “a tail then a head”, “two tails” is exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so it is a legitimate sample space. Its members carry probabilities $1/2$, $1/4$ and $1/4$: they group the equally likely ordered outcomes as $\{HH,HT\}$, $\{TH\}$ and $\{TT\}$. This calculation also appears in the interpretations deck. Mutual exclusivity is a requirement on the sample space; it says nothing about the probabilities assigned to its elements, and counting the members is valid only when they happen to be equally probable.

### The same reading in the Bertrand construction

The sampling procedures in Section 3 produce a geometric chord almost surely. After excluding the stated null cases, we may describe their outputs on the common space $\mathcal C_*$ of nondegenerate, nondiameter chords. In this output description, a chord is an elementary outcome. The three rotationally invariant models use the same chord space and event collection but different probability measures. Their original sampling outcomes can instead be angles, distances or points; Section 3 distinguishes these descriptions.

The event $E=\{c:L(c)>\sqrt3R\}$ is not an outcome. It is a set containing uncountably many chords, and it is assigned a probability as a set.

This last point also marks the limit of the summation rule above. In a continuous model each individual outcome has probability zero, so

$$\sum_{c\in E}P(\{c\})=0\ne P(E),$$

and the probability of $E$ cannot be recovered by adding the probabilities of the outcomes it contains. Countable additivity is additivity over countably many disjoint events, and $E$ is not a countable union of its singletons. The rule $P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}P(\{\omega\})$ applies to countable events with measurable singletons; it does not extend to an uncountable event by countable additivity.

### Event collections and the probability triplet

The main notes use all subsets as events for finite experiments. Here are the precise requirements for a general triplet $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$.

::: {.callout-note title="Definitions: power set and sigma-algebra"}
The power set $\mathcal P(\Omega)=2^\Omega=\{E:E\subseteq\Omega\}$ contains every subset, including $\varnothing$ and $\Omega$. For finite $|\Omega|=n$, it has $2^n$ elements, since including or excluding each outcome gives two choices. An event collection $\mathcal F$ is a subset of $\mathcal P(\Omega)$, so its members are themselves subsets of $\Omega$.

The event collection $\mathcal F$ must be a **sigma-algebra** on $\Omega$.
Its requirements are:

1. **Contains the sample space:** $\Omega\in\mathcal F$.
2. **Closed under complements:** if $E\in\mathcal F$, then
   $E^c=\Omega\setminus E\in\mathcal F$.
3. **Closed under countable unions:** if $E_1,E_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F$,
   then $\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}E_i\in\mathcal F$.

These conditions ensure that “not $E$” and “at least one of
$E_1,E_2,\ldots$” are events whenever the component sets are events. Since
this example has a finite sample space, taking $\mathcal F=2^\Omega$, the
power set, satisfies all three requirements.


No disjointness assumption is needed for closure under unions. It is needed when applying countable additivity of probability. Closure also gives $\varnothing\in\mathcal F$, countable intersections by De Morgan's law, and differences $E\setminus F=E\cap F^c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="The three probability axioms"}
For events in $\mathcal F$:

$$P(E)\ge0,\qquad P(\Omega)=1,$$

and, for pairwise disjoint $E_1,E_2,\ldots$,

$$P\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\right)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(E_n).$$

Pairwise disjoint means $E_i\cap E_j=\varnothing$ for $i\ne j$. This assumption is needed to add probabilities without double-counting; it is not needed for sigma-algebra closure under unions.
:::


Two familiar properties follow rather than being separate axioms. Additivity for $\Omega$ and $\varnothing$ gives $1=1+P(\varnothing)$, hence $P(\varnothing)=0$. Additivity for $E$ and $E^c$ gives

$$P(E)+P(E^c)=1.$$

Nonnegativity then gives $P(E)\le1$. More generally, inclusion $E\subseteq F$ implies $P(E)\le P(F)$ by splitting $F$ into $E$ and $F\setminus E$.

The axioms do not impose uniformity. On a finite space, any nonnegative singleton weights summing to 1 define a probability measure on the full power set by addition.

### Worked example: a die observed through two LEDs {#sensor-sigma-algebra}

Roll a stipulated fair six-sided die, but suppose a sensor displays only two binary readings. The red LED lights for

$$A=\{1,2\},$$

and the green LED lights for

$$B=\{2,3,4\}.$$

Let $X=\mathbf1_A$ and $Y=\mathbf1_B$: each indicator is 1 when its event occurs and 0 otherwise.

| Die outcome $\omega$ | Red $X(\omega)$ | Green $Y(\omega)$ | Sensor reading |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 1 | 0 | Red only |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | Both LEDs |
| 3 | 0 | 1 | Green only |
| 4 | 0 | 1 | Green only |
| 5 | 0 | 0 | Neither LED |
| 6 | 0 | 0 | Neither LED |

What can we determine from the sensor? Both LEDs identify outcome 2. Green alone identifies the group $\{3,4\}$, but not the individual face. In particular, **outcome 3 lights only the green LED**.

The four distinguishable groups are

$$C_{10}=\{1\},\quad C_{11}=\{2\},\quad
C_{01}=\{3,4\},\quad C_{00}=\{5,6\}.$$

Under the fair-die assumption, their probabilities are $1/6,1/6,1/3,1/3$ respectively. They are disjoint, cover the six outcomes, and have probabilities summing to 1.

The events $A$ and $B$ are not complements. They overlap at outcome 2, and their union omits outcomes 5 and 6:

$$A\cap B=\{2\},\qquad A\cup B=\{1,2,3,4\}.$$

Thus

$$P(A\cup B)=\frac26+\frac36-\frac16=\frac46.$$

This calculation motivates the distinction between the selected die face, an event containing several faces, and the information available from the readings.

### The sensor sigma-algebra and the full model

Every event decidable from the LED pair must include or exclude an entire indistinguishable group. If it included 3 but excluded 4, the green-only reading would not determine whether that event occurred.

Consequently the sensor collection consists of all unions of

$$\{1\},\quad\{2\},\quad\{3,4\},\quad\{5,6\}.$$

These groups are the **atoms** of this finite event collection: its nonempty events that cannot be split into smaller nonempty events within the collection. They are not necessarily individual outcomes.

Write

$$\mathcal G=\sigma(X,Y)=\sigma(A,B)
=\left\{\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal J}C:
\mathcal J\subseteq\{C_{10},C_{11},C_{01},C_{00}\}\right\}.$$

The empty choice gives $\varnothing$, and choosing all four gives $\Omega$. There are $2^4=16$ distinct events. Complements select the remaining atoms; unions select any atom appearing in a constituent event. These operations stay within the collection, including countable unions, so $\mathcal G$ is a sigma-algebra.

The notation $\sigma(A,B)$ means the smallest sigma-algebra containing $A$ and $B$. It must contain their four intersections with complements,

$$A\cap B^c,\quad A\cap B,\quad A^c\cap B,\quad A^c\cap B^c,$$

which are precisely the four atoms above. It therefore contains all their unions. Conversely, that collection of unions is already a sigma-algebra containing $A$ and $B$, establishing that it is the smallest one.

#### Is $\{3\}$ impossible, or does its probability fail to exist?

Neither follows from the sensor restriction. Keep the two models explicit:

| Model | Event collection | Does it assign a probability to $\{3\}$? |
|---|---|---|
| Full fair-die model $(\Omega,\mathcal P(\Omega),P)$ | All 64 subsets | Yes: $P(\{3\})=1/6$ |
| Sensor model $(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ | The 16 unions of sensor atoms | No: $\{3\}\notin\mathcal G$ |

Here $P|_{\mathcal G}$ is the **restriction** of the original measure: retain its values only for events in $\mathcal G$. It assigns

$$P|_{\mathcal G}(\{3,4\})=\frac13,$$

but $P|_{\mathcal G}(\{3\})$ is undefined because $\{3\}$ is outside its domain. It is not zero.

The fair-die model still permits inference about the hidden face. For instance, it gives

$$P(\{3\}\mid\{3,4\})=\frac{1/6}{1/3}=\frac12.$$

This inference uses the full model and its fairness assumption. It does not mean that the sensor can identify whether 3 occurred.

#### The observation does not determine a hidden probability split

Even knowing the probabilities of all four sensor readings does not identify how their masses are divided within $\{3,4\}$ or $\{5,6\}$. For example, these two full-space assignments agree on every event in $\mathcal G$:

| Face | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Fair assignment $P$ | $1/6$ | $1/6$ | $1/6$ | $1/6$ | $1/6$ | $1/6$ |
| Alternative assignment $Q$ | $1/6$ | $1/6$ | $0$ | $1/3$ | $1/6$ | $1/6$ |

They both give green-only probability $1/3$, yet disagree on $\{3\}$. The alternative is not fair; it demonstrates what the sensor-reading distribution alone cannot establish. Fairness is additional model information.

::: {.callout-note title="Measurability versus observability"}
In general, a sigma-algebra specifies the domain of a probability measure. It need not come from a physical sensor. When it is generated by observations, it describes event statements decidable from those observations. An event can be measurable in a fuller model while being indistinguishable using a particular sensor. Neither exclusion from a smaller sigma-algebra nor probability zero should be confused with logical impossibility.
:::


### A continuous triplet on the unit interval {#unit-interval-triplet}

Suppose a simulation selects a number uniformly from the unit interval. What is the probability that the selected value lies between $1/4$ and $3/4$? Uniformity means that an interval's probability is its length, so the answer should be $3/4-1/4=1/2$. To make this a probability model, we must specify more than intervals: “outside this interval” and “in at least one of these intervals” must also be events.

Take $\Omega_u=[0,1]$. A sample point $u\in[0,1]$ is a number; an event is a suitable **set of numbers**. We use the Borel σ-algebra

$$\mathcal F_u=\mathcal B([0,1])
=\sigma\bigl(\{(a,b)\cap[0,1]:a,b\in\mathbb R,\ a<b\}\bigr).$$

Here $\sigma(\mathcal A)$ means the smallest σ-algebra containing every member of a family $\mathcal A$. Equivalently, it is the intersection of all σ-algebras on $[0,1]$ that contain that family. Such σ-algebras exist because the power set $2^{[0,1]}$ is one of them. The intervals intersected with $[0,1]$ generate all the relatively open sets of the unit interval.

A **Borel set** is one member of $\mathcal B([0,1])$. The **Borel σ-algebra** is the collection of all those members. For example,

$$[1/4,3/4]\in\mathcal B([0,1]),\qquad [1/4,3/4]\subseteq[0,1].$$

The first statement says it is a measurable event; the second says its elements are possible outcomes.

#### What the Borel σ-algebra contains

It contains $\varnothing$, $[0,1]$, every relatively open or closed subset, every interval within $[0,1]$ (including half-open intervals), and every singleton $\{u\}$. It is closed under complements **relative to $[0,1]$**, countable unions and countable intersections. The intersection property follows from De Morgan's law:

$$\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n
=[0,1]\setminus\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl([0,1]\setminus E_n\bigr).$$

For example, each set $[0,1]\cap(u-1/n,u+1/n)$ is relatively open, and

$$\{u\}=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl([0,1]\cap(u-1/n,u+1/n)\bigr).$$

Thus singletons are Borel. Every countable set of points in $[0,1]$ is then Borel, being a countable union of singletons. In particular, $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$ is Borel, as is its complement, the irrational points in $[0,1]$.

These examples do not exhaust the collection: The collection includes sets formed through repeated countable unions, intersections and complements, beyond the examples listed. Closure under **countable** operations does not imply closure under arbitrary uncountable unions. The Borel σ-algebra is smaller than $2^{[0,1]}$; not every subset is Borel. Section 5 below constructs a set that is not Lebesgue measurable. Since every Borel set is Lebesgue measurable, that set is not Borel either.

#### Assigning probabilities and checking the triplet

Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure, the standard measure that assigns each interval its length, and restrict it to Borel subsets of $[0,1]$:

$$P_u(E)=\lambda(E),\qquad E\in\mathcal B([0,1]).$$

No scaling is needed because $\lambda([0,1])=1$. Our triplet is

$$\bigl([0,1],\mathcal B([0,1]),P_u\bigr).$$

To verify it, check the event collection and the measure separately.

- **Event collection.** Every σ-algebra in the defining intersection contains $[0,1]$ and is closed under relative complements and countable unions. Their intersection inherits these properties, so $\mathcal B([0,1])$ is a σ-algebra.
- **Nonnegativity.** Lebesgue measure is nonnegative, so $P_u(E)\ge0$ for each Borel event $E$.
- **Normalization.** $P_u([0,1])=\lambda([0,1])=1$.
- **Countable additivity.** For pairwise disjoint Borel events $E_1,E_2,\ldots$, the countable additivity of Lebesgue measure gives

  $$P_u\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\right)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P_u(E_n).$$

Here we use the standard theorem that Lebesgue measure exists and is countably additive on Borel sets. Checking a few intervals alone would not establish that theorem. Restricting this measure to the unit interval verifies all the probability axioms, and $P_u(E)\le1$ follows from $E\subseteq[0,1]$.

#### Worked events in the triplet

| Borel event $E$ | Probability $P_u(E)$ | Reason |
|---|---:|---|
| $[1/4,3/4]$ | $1/2$ | Interval length |
| $[0,1/4)\cup(3/4,1]$ | $1/2$ | Complement of the preceding event |
| $\{1/2\}$ | $0$ | A singleton has zero length |
| $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$ | $0$ | Countably many disjoint singletons of measure zero |
| $[0,1]\setminus\mathbb Q$ | $1$ | Complement of the rational points |

The rational points are dense in $[0,1]$, but still have probability zero in this model. The measure is length, not the number of points or how closely they are spaced.

For an explicit countable-additivity calculation, let

$$I_n=(2^{-(n+1)},2^{-n}],\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.$$

These Borel intervals are pairwise disjoint and have union $(0,1]$. Hence

$$P_u((0,1])=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^{-(n+1)}=1.$$

Adding the zero-probability singleton $\{0\}$ gives $P_u([0,1])=1$. This example illustrates countable additivity. It does not license an uncountable sum of singleton probabilities.

We can also use the larger Lebesgue sigma-algebra $\mathcal L([0,1])$, obtained by completing Borel length: include every subset of a Borel set of length zero. This does not include every subset of the interval. Section 5 explains the obstruction for standard length.

### Why countable operations matter

On a finite space, a countable union can involve only finitely many distinct subsets. On $[0,1]$, infinite sequences of events give genuinely new constructions. For example,

$$A_n=[0,1-1/n],\quad n\ge2,
\qquad \bigcup_{n=2}^{\infty}A_n=[0,1),$$

and

$$B_n=[0,1/n],\quad n\ge1,
\qquad \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}B_n=\{0\}.$$

Under uniform length, the first sequence has probabilities tending to 1, while the second has probabilities tending to 0. Countable additivity implies **continuity of probability**: for increasing events the probability of the union is the limit of their probabilities, and for decreasing events in a probability space the probability of the intersection is their limit. Thus the singleton $\{0\}$ has probability zero even though 0 remains a possible sample point.

This explains why closure under finite combinations alone would not suffice for the usual treatment of limiting events.

## 2. Random variables, inverse images and probability laws

On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, a real-valued **random variable** is a measurable function

$$X:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Measurability means that $X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F$ for every Borel set $B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. The Borel σ-algebra is generated by open intervals and includes the intervals, singleton sets and their countable combinations used here. For a real-valued function, it is sufficient to check $\{\omega:X(\omega)\le x\}\in\mathcal F$ for every real $x$.

### The distinction between a random variable and a set function

A random variable is a function **on outcomes**, not a real-valued set function on events. It induces the following map between collections of sets:

$$X^{-1}:\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\longrightarrow\mathcal F,\qquad
B\longmapsto\{\omega:X(\omega)\in B\}.$$

The probability measure and the distribution of $X$ are real-valued **set functions**:

$$P:\mathcal F\to[0,1],\qquad P_X:\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\to[0,1],$$

$$P_X(B)=P\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr)=P(X\in B).$$

Thus a numerical question about $X$ is first converted to a set of outcomes, and that event is assigned a probability. This is the set-based construction used in the Bertrand calculation below. It follows the distinction in Jagannathan, Chapter 11, Definitions 68–70.

### Independence used in the examples

Events $E,F$ are independent when $P(E\cap F)=P(E)P(F)$. Random variables
$U,V$ are independent when this identity holds for the events $\{U\in A\}$
and $\{V\in B\}$ for every pair of Borel sets $A,B$. For variables with a
joint density on a product domain, $f_{U,V}(u,v)=f_U(u)f_V(v)$ almost everywhere
implies independence: integrating over $A\times B$ separates into the product
of the two marginal integrals. Independent fair tosses below stipulate the
product measure, giving each ordered pair mass $(1/2)(1/2)=1/4$.

### Worked example: the head count

For two independent fair tosses, each outcome in $\Omega=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}$ has probability $1/4$, and $\mathcal F=2^\Omega$. Define $X(HH)=2$, $X(HT)=X(TH)=1$, and $X(TT)=0$. Then

$$P_X(\{1\})=P(\{HT,TH\})=1/2,$$

$$P_X([1,2])=P(\{HH,HT,TH\})=3/4.$$

The distribution assigns probabilities $1/4,1/2,1/4$ to $0,1,2$. It is obtained through inverse images, not by assuming that the three numerical values are equally likely.

### Worked example: an indicator

For an event $A\in\mathcal F$, its indicator is the random variable

$$\mathbf1_A(\omega)=\begin{cases}1,&\omega\in A,\\0,&\omega\notin A.\end{cases}$$

Its inverse images satisfy $\mathbf1_A^{-1}(\{1\})=A$ and $\mathbf1_A^{-1}(\{0\})=A^c$. Consequently, $P(\mathbf1_A=1)=P(A)$.

For the parity model in the [event-collection lab](../materials/01-probability/lab.html#events), take $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\{2,4,6\},\{1,3,5\},\Omega\}$. The indicator of an even face is measurable. The numerical face-value function is not measurable relative to that σ-algebra, since the inverse image of $\{6\}$ is the unavailable subset $\{6\}$.

### Measurability and the probability law

Return to the six-ticket audit of Section 1, with $B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\}$, $X_B=\mathbf1_B$, and $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega\}$.

To calculate $P(X_B\in D)$, the inverse image $X_B^{-1}(D)$ must be an event.
For example, $X_B^{-1}((1/2,3/2))=B\in\mathcal F$, giving probability $1/2$.
This requirement motivates the formal definition.

As with the unit interval in Section 1, now on $\mathbb R$, the **Borel σ-algebra** $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ is the smallest
sigma-algebra containing all open intervals. It includes intervals,
singletons and their countable unions, intersections and complements.
A function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is **measurable**, and hence a real-valued
random variable on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, if

$$X^{-1}(D)\in\mathcal F\quad\text{for every }D\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).$$

Its **law** or **distribution** is the probability measure

$$P_X(D)=P(X^{-1}(D)),\qquad D\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).$$

In the full finite model every function is measurable because all subsets
are events. For $X_B$, the inverse image is one of $\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega$
according to whether $D$ contains neither of 0 and 1, only 1, only 0, or both.
Thus $X_B$ is measurable even for the smaller collection $\mathcal G$.
Its law assigns mass $1/2$ each to 0 and 1. By contrast, the ID-code function
$J(t_i)=i$ is not measurable for $\mathcal G$: $J^{-1}(\{1\})=\{t_1\}$ is
unavailable in that collection. It is measurable for $2^\Omega$.

### What a random variable generates {#generated-sigma-algebra}

The pair of LED readings separates the four groups in the LED example above. A single numerical recording similarly determines an event collection. The qualification is that it determines the **smallest** compatible collection, not necessarily the full collection of the model.

::: {.callout-note title="Precise statement"}
Given a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, with Borel sets as the events on its numerical output space, define

$$\boxed{\sigma(X)=\{X^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}.}$$

Here $X^{-1}(B)=\{\omega:X(\omega)\in B\}$ is an inverse image, not an inverse function. The collection is the smallest sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ making $X$ measurable.

If a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is already specified, $X$ is a random variable on it precisely when $\sigma(X)\subseteq\mathcal F$. Equality is not required. Also, $X$ alone does not determine $P$.
:::


Why is this collection a sigma-algebra? The inverse image of $\mathbb R$ is $\Omega$, and inverse images preserve complements and countable unions:

$$X^{-1}(B^c)=\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr)^c,\qquad
X^{-1}\left(\bigcup_n B_n\right)=\bigcup_n X^{-1}(B_n).$$

Any event collection making $X$ measurable must contain all these inverse images, establishing minimality. In particular, we can begin with a numerical function and construct $\sigma(X)$; to call it a random variable on an existing model, we must check compatibility with that model's $\mathcal F$.

Also distinguish $\sigma(X)$ from the **distribution** $P_X(B)=P(X\in B)$. The former is a collection of events on the original outcome space $\Omega$; the latter assigns probabilities to Borel sets of numerical values in $\mathbb R$ and depends on the chosen $P$.

The generated sigma-algebra consists of the Borel-event questions answerable from observing $X$. For a finite-valued function, its nonempty level sets $\{X=x\}$ form a partition, and $\sigma(X)$ consists of all unions of those level sets. That finite partition rule is what makes the following examples easy to work out.

#### Parity as a special case

For the indicator $H=\mathbf1_{\{2,4,6\}}$, the two level sets are even and odd, so

$$\sigma(H)=\{\varnothing,\{2,4,6\},\{1,3,5\},\Omega\}.$$

The identity function $J(\omega)=\omega$ instead generates the full power set. On the full fair-die model both are random variables; on the parity-only model $J$ is not measurable, since $J^{-1}(\{3\})=\{3\}$ is not an available event. A numerical assignment becomes a random variable on a specified model only when it satisfies this measurability requirement.

### Worked example: three service-response categories

Consider eight hypothetical fixed service-request IDs. For this new experiment, take $\Omega=\{r_1,\ldots,r_8\}$. Select one uniformly and record only its response-time category. The thresholds are stipulated for this teaching example.

| Request IDs | Recorded category | Numerical code $Z$ |
|---|---|---:|
| $r_1,r_2$ | Fast: less than 100 ms | 0 |
| $r_3,r_4,r_5$ | Standard: 100–500 ms inclusive | 1 |
| $r_6,r_7,r_8$ | Slow: more than 500 ms | 2 |

Write the three level sets as

$$C_0=\{r_1,r_2\},\quad C_1=\{r_3,r_4,r_5\},\quad C_2=\{r_6,r_7,r_8\}.$$

Knowing $Z$ identifies one of these groups but not an individual request within it. Each union of groups is answerable from the category. Consequently,

$$\sigma(Z)=\{\varnothing,C_0,C_1,C_2,
C_0\cup C_1,C_0\cup C_2,C_1\cup C_2,\Omega\}.$$

There are $2^3=8$ events, compared with $2^8=256$ in the full power set of request IDs. In particular, $C_0$ and $C_1$ are not complements: $C_0^c=C_1\cup C_2$.

#### Two overlapping events that are not complements

Let

$$A=\{Z\le1\}=C_0\cup C_1\quad\text{(not slow)},$$

$$B=\{Z\ge1\}=C_1\cup C_2\quad\text{(not fast)}.$$

Then

$$A\cap B=C_1,\qquad A\cup B=\Omega,\qquad
A^c=C_2,\qquad B^c=C_0.$$

Neither event is the other's complement: they overlap on every standard-response request. Under uniform ID selection,

$$P(A)=\frac58,\qquad P(B)=\frac68=\frac34,
\qquad P(A\cap B)=\frac38.$$

The union calculation checks:

$$P(A\cup B)=\frac58+\frac68-\frac38=1.$$

The category probabilities are $1/4,3/8,3/8$. These numbers come from the sampling rule, not from the fact that there are three categories. Under a different weighting of request IDs, the same function $Z$ would generate exactly the same sigma-algebra but could have a different distribution.

#### Building the collection from two event questions instead

Suppose the dashboard originally answers only “not slow?” and “not fast?” The answers are the two indicators $\mathbf1_A,\mathbf1_B$. Together they distinguish:

| Pair of indicator values | Identified group |
|---|---|
| $(1,0)$ | $C_0$ |
| $(1,1)$ | $C_1$ |
| $(0,1)$ | $C_2$ |
| $(0,0)$ | Empty: impossible under these categories |

Thus

$$\sigma(A,B)=\sigma(\mathbf1_A,\mathbf1_B)=\sigma(Z).$$

This is a useful way to teach closure: start with two questions that overlap, identify the groups their answers distinguish, and then take all unions of those groups. Each single binary observation gives at most four events; two jointly observed indicators can retain more information.

## 3. Bertrand's paradox: sampling maps and induced distributions

This section develops the Bertrand question posed in Section 3 of the main notes. What is the probability that a randomly generated chord is longer than the side of an inscribed equilateral triangle? We first calculate three answers to this same plain-English question. Only then do we use the Kolmogorov triplet to identify precisely which probability problem each calculation answers.

### The paradox: one question, three answers

For the unit circle, a chord at distance $r$ from the centre has length

$$L=2\sqrt{1-r^2}.$$

Thus $L>\sqrt3$ exactly when $r<1/2$, or equivalently when the chord intersects the interior of the concentric disk of radius $1/2$.

Consider three plausible readings of “choose a chord at random.”

1. **Choose its angle uniformly at a fixed endpoint.** Fix $a=(1,0)$ and measure an angle $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ from the upward tangent towards the disk. The resulting chord has length $2\sin\,\theta$. It is longer than $\sqrt3$ when $\pi/3<\theta<2\pi/3$, an interval occupying one third of the available angular range. The answer is **$1/3$**.
2. **Choose its distance from the centre uniformly.** Fix the midpoint direction and choose its distance $r$ uniformly between 0 and 1. Draw the chord perpendicular to that radius. The favorable distances satisfy $r<1/2$, half the available range. The answer is **$1/2$**.
3. **Choose its midpoint uniformly in disk area.** Draw the chord perpendicular to the radius through the chosen midpoint. It is long enough exactly when the midpoint lies inside the concentric disk of radius $1/2$. That disk occupies one quarter of the total area. The answer is **$1/4$**. The centre and boundary are zero-area exceptions handled below.

We have asked the same question in words and obtained

$$\frac13,\qquad\frac12,\qquad\frac14.$$

Each calculation is correct for its construction. The phrase “a random chord” leaves the sampling rule unspecified: uniform angle, distance and area are different assumptions. We now use the Kolmogorov triplet to resolve the apparent contradiction.

### Making the experiments precise with the Kolmogorov triplet

A probability model is a triplet $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$: $\Omega$ specifies the outcomes, $\mathcal F$ specifies the measurable events, and $P$ assigns their probabilities. We now identify these three components for each calculation. We distinguish the common geometric question from the event that represents it in each sampling space.

**Experiment I: a uniform angle at a fixed endpoint.** Fix the endpoint $a=(1,0)$. From the upward tangent at $a$, measure $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ towards the interior of the disk. The ray has direction $(-\sin\,\theta,\cos\,\theta)$; its second intersection with the circle defines the chord. Substituting $a+\ell(-\sin\,\theta,\cos\,\theta)$ into the circle equation gives $\ell(\ell-2\sin\,\theta)=0$, so its length is $L=2\sin\,\theta$.

Choose $\theta$ uniformly. The triplet and measure are

$$\Omega_1=(0,\pi),\qquad \mathcal F_1=\mathcal B((0,\pi)),\qquad
P_1(B)=\frac1\pi\int_B d\theta\quad(B\in\mathcal F_1).$$

Here $\mathcal B$ is the Borel σ-algebra, generated by the open subsets of the stated domain. The favorable event and probability are

$$E_1=(\pi/3,2\pi/3),\qquad P_1(E_1)=\frac{2\pi/3-\pi/3}{\pi}=\frac13.$$

The endpoints $\theta=0,\pi$ would give zero-length chords and have been excluded. The diameter at $\theta=\pi/2$ has probability zero and will also be omitted when we introduce the common chord chart.

**Experiment II: a uniform distance with a fixed direction.** Choose $r\in(0,1)$ uniformly, set the midpoint to $(r,0)$, and draw the vertical chord through it. Specifying the midpoint direction makes the chord unique; distance alone determines only its length.

$$\Omega_2=(0,1),\qquad \mathcal F_2=\mathcal B((0,1)),\qquad
P_2(B)=\int_B dr\quad(B\in\mathcal F_2).$$

The favorable event and probability are

$$E_2=(0,1/2),\qquad P_2(E_2)=\int_0^{1/2}dr=\frac12.$$

**Experiment III: a uniform midpoint in area.** Choose a point $M=(x,y)$ uniformly in the disk and draw the chord perpendicular to $OM$ through $M$. To make this construction unique and nondegenerate everywhere on its domain, exclude the centre and boundary, both of which have area zero. Put

$$D^*=\{(x,y):0<x^2+y^2<1\}.$$

Then

$$\Omega_3=D^*,\qquad \mathcal F_3=\mathcal B(D^*),\qquad
P_3(B)=\frac1\pi\iint_B dx\,dy\quad(B\in\mathcal F_3).$$

The favorable event is the punctured inner disk, so

$$E_3=\{(x,y):0<x^2+y^2<1/4\},\qquad
P_3(E_3)=\frac{\pi(1/2)^2}{\pi}=\frac14.$$

Deleting the centre does not change either area. Using the closed disk with an explicit convention for the exceptional cases gives the same probabilities.

| Experiment | Sample space | Measure on Borel events | Favorable event | Probability |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| Fixed endpoint, uniform angle | $(0,\pi)$ | $d\theta/\pi$ | $\pi/3<\theta<2\pi/3$ | $1/3$ |
| Fixed direction, uniform distance | $(0,1)$ | $dr$ | $r<1/2$ | $1/2$ |
| Uniform midpoint area | $D^*$ | $dx\,dy/\pi$ | $x^2+y^2<1/4$ | $1/4$ |

The notation for the measures in the table means integration over an event, as defined above. **With the probability triplets specified, the apparent contradiction is resolved:** the three answers belong to three different probability models.

### Advanced: measures on a common chord space

The triplets above complete the resolution. The remaining calculations study sampling maps and induced measures on geometric chords. They are not needed to resolve the paradox.

We consider three rotationally invariant models independently:

- **Model A:** choose two independent uniform endpoints on the circumference.
- **Model B:** choose a uniform radial distance and an independent uniform midpoint direction.
- **Model C:** choose a midpoint uniformly in disk area.

Their connection to Experiments I–III is Exercise 8. In particular, equal chord-length distributions need not mean equal measures on geometric chords. A common sample space does not require identical supports.

The endpoint, distance and area constructions are also discussed in Larson and Odoni, [*Urban Operations Research*, §3.3.2](https://web.mit.edu/urban_or_book/www/book/chapter3/3.3.2a.html). We now specify the common measurable space and derive each model's sampling law.

### The event and a common chord space

Fix a circle of radius $R>0$. The side of an inscribed equilateral triangle has length $\sqrt3R$. For a chord $c$, define the real-valued random variables

$$D(c)=\text{distance from the centre to }c,\qquad T(c)=D(c)/R,\qquad L(c)=\text{length of }c.$$

The geometry gives

$$L(c)=2R\sqrt{1-T(c)^2},\qquad E=\{c:L(c)>\sqrt3R\}=\{c:T(c)<1/2\}.$$

We compare the probability of this **same event** under three probability measures on a common chord space.

For a one-to-one parametrization, let $\mathcal C_*$ be the set of unordered, nondegenerate chords that are not diameters. Coincident-endpoint chords and diameters have probability zero under all three rules below. Excluding them makes the inverse formulas unambiguous without changing any calculated probability. They may instead be retained in an enlarged space with total probability zero.

### A chord parametrization and its inverse

Let $0<t<1$ and $0\le\phi<2\pi$. Write

$$n(\phi)=(\cos\,\phi,\sin\,\phi),\qquad n_\perp(\phi)=(-\sin\,\phi,\cos\,\phi).$$

Define $C(\phi,t)$ to be the chord with unordered endpoints

$$z_\pm=Rt\,n(\phi)\ \pm\ R\sqrt{1-t^2}\,n_\perp(\phi).$$

Its midpoint is $m=Rt\,n(\phi)$, so the inverse is

$$C^{-1}(c)=\left(\operatorname{Arg}(m),\frac{\|m\|}{R}\right),\qquad m=\frac{z_++z_-}{2}.$$

Here $\operatorname{Arg}$ is chosen in $[0,2\pi)$. The midpoint is nonzero because diameters were excluded. Hence $C:[0,2\pi)\times(0,1)\to\mathcal C_*$ is a bijection. Write $K=[0,2\pi)\times(0,1)$ and define the event collection explicitly by

$$\mathcal F_{\mathcal C_*}=\{B\subseteq\mathcal C_*:C^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal B(K)\}.$$

This makes $C$ and its inverse measurable. The three chord-space triplets are

$$(\mathcal C_*,\mathcal F_{\mathcal C_*},P_A),\qquad
(\mathcal C_*,\mathcal F_{\mathcal C_*},P_B),\qquad
(\mathcal C_*,\mathcal F_{\mathcal C_*},P_C).$$

Their sample space, event collection and long-chord event $E$ are identical; their measures differ. The sampling maps below define these measures.

The length function $L$ is **not** a bijection on chords: all orientations with the same $t$ have the same length. The inverse image $L^{-1}(B)$ is still defined for every Borel set of lengths $B$.

### A common source of uniform samples

Use the probability space

$$\Omega_0=(0,1)\times[0,1),\qquad\mathcal F_0=\mathcal B(\Omega_0),\qquad Q=\text{uniform area measure on }\Omega_0.$$

The coordinate random variables $U(u,v)=u$ and $V(u,v)=v$ are independent uniform variables. Endpoints of these intervals have measure zero. For each mechanism $j\in\{A,B,C\}$, define a sampling map

$$\Psi_j(u,v)=C\bigl(2\pi v,q_j(u)\bigr).$$

Each $q_j$ given below is a continuous bijection of $(0,1)$. Since $C^{-1}\circ\Psi_j(u,v)=(2\pi v,q_j(u))$ is continuous into $K$, the definition of $\mathcal F_{\mathcal C_*}$ makes $\Psi_j$ measurable. It is also a bijection onto $\mathcal C_*$. The event $E$ is measurable because $C^{-1}(E)=[0,2\pi)\times(0,1/2)$.

The induced probability measure on chord events is

$$P_j(F)=Q\bigl(\Psi_j^{-1}(F)\bigr),\qquad F\in\mathcal F_{\mathcal C_*}.$$

The chord-length random variable on the uniform source space is $L_j=L\circ\Psi_j$. We now specify each $q_j$, its inverse and the distribution it produces.

### A. Two independent uniform endpoints

The original procedure selects independent angles $A_1,A_2\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,2\pi)$ and joins the points $R(\cos\, A_i,\sin\, A_i)$. The joint angle density is $1/(2\pi)^2$.

Let $\delta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ be the signed principal difference $A_2-A_1$ modulo $2\pi$, and let $H=|\delta|/2$. In the deck's notation, $\alpha=|\delta|=2H$. The cases $\delta=0$ (coincident endpoints) and $|\delta|=\pi$ (diameters) have probability zero and are excluded for the chord chart. The map $(a_1,a_2)\mapsto(a_1,\delta)$ is a bijection apart from this null boundary and the angular wrap. For each $a_1$, the second coordinate is a translation modulo $2\pi$, so the map preserves area. Hence $(A_1,\delta)$ has constant density $1/(4\pi^2)$ on the rectangle.

Now define $\Phi=(A_1+\delta/2)\bmod 2\pi$. The map $(a_1,\delta)\mapsto(\Phi,\delta)$ is also one-to-one on the chosen half-open angular ranges and preserves area: for fixed $\delta$ it is a translation in the first coordinate. Thus $(\Phi,\delta)$ has the same constant density, which factors into uniform marginal densities. Applying $H=|\delta|/2$ gives the joint density

$$f_{\Phi,H}(\phi,h)=\frac1{2\pi}\,\frac2\pi,\qquad 0\le\phi<2\pi,\quad 0<h<\pi/2.$$

Therefore $\Phi$ and $H$ are independent, $\Phi$ is uniform, and $H\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,\pi/2)$. The midpoint is in direction $\Phi$, since the midpoint vector is proportional to $\cos\,(H)\,n(\Phi)$ and $\cos\,(H)>0$ almost surely.

The ordered-endpoint map is two-to-one because interchanging endpoints leaves the chord unchanged. Its inverse therefore recovers an **unordered pair**, not a unique ordered pair. From $(\phi,t)$, put $h=\arccos(t)$; the unordered endpoint angles are

$$\{(\phi-h)\bmod 2\pi,\ (\phi+h)\bmod 2\pi\}.$$

Thus an equivalent, bijective sampling parametrization of the unordered chords uses $U=2H/\pi$ and $V=\Phi/(2\pi)$:

$$q_A(u)=\cos\,(\pi u/2),\qquad\Psi_A^{-1}(c)=\left(\frac2\pi\arccos(T(c)),\frac{\operatorname{Arg}(m)}{2\pi}\right).$$

The length random variable and the inverse image of the event are

$$L_A(u,v)=2R\sin\,(\pi u/2),\qquad\Psi_A^{-1}(E)=\{(u,v):u>2/3\}.$$

Consequently,

$$P_A(E)=Q(U>2/3)=1/3.$$

For $0<t<1$, the induced distribution of normalized midpoint distance is

$$F_{T,A}(t)=1-\frac2\pi\arccos(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin(t),\qquad f_{T,A}(t)=\frac{2}{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}}.$$

It is not uniform in radial distance.

### B. Uniform radial distance

Choose $D\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,R)$ and an independent direction $\Phi\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,2\pi)$. Construct the perpendicular chord through $D\,n(\Phi)$. Equivalently,

$$q_B(u)=u,\qquad\Psi_B^{-1}(c)=\left(T(c),\frac{\operatorname{Arg}(m)}{2\pi}\right).$$

The original $(D,\Phi)$ joint density is $1/(2\pi R)$ on $(0,R)\times[0,2\pi)$. In normalized coordinates, $T$ has density $f_{T,B}(t)=1$ and distribution function $F_{T,B}(t)=t$ for $0<t<1$.

$$L_B(u,v)=2R\sqrt{1-u^2},\qquad\Psi_B^{-1}(E)=\{(u,v):u<1/2\}.$$

Therefore

$$P_B(E)=Q(U<1/2)=1/2.$$

### C. Uniform midpoint in disk area

Choose a midpoint $M=(M_1,M_2)$ with Cartesian density $1/(\pi R^2)$ inside the disk. In polar coordinates $M=Rt\,n(\phi)$, the area element is $R^2t\,dt\,d\phi$. Hence

$$f_{T,\Phi}(t,\phi)=\frac{t}{\pi}=2t\cdot\frac1{2\pi},\qquad 0<t<1.$$

Thus $T$ and $\Phi$ are independent, $\Phi$ is uniform, and $T$ has density $2t$ and distribution function $F_{T,C}(t)=t^2$ for $0<t<1$. A uniform draw $U$ is transformed by

$$q_C(u)=\sqrt u,\qquad\Psi_C^{-1}(c)=\left(T(c)^2,\frac{\operatorname{Arg}(m)}{2\pi}\right).$$

The length random variable and event preimage are

$$L_C(u,v)=2R\sqrt{1-u},\qquad\Psi_C^{-1}(E)=\{(u,v):u<1/4\}.$$

Therefore

$$P_C(E)=Q(U<1/4)=1/4.$$

The area ratio $\pi(R/2)^2/(\pi R^2)$ gives the same result.

### Explicit comparison on the same coordinates

In every model, $\Phi$ is independent of $T$ and uniform on $[0,2\pi)$. The density with respect to $d\phi\,dt$ is $f_{T,j}(t)/(2\pi)$. Thus, for every $B\in\mathcal F_{\mathcal C_*}$,

$$P_j(B)=\iint_{C^{-1}(B)}\frac{f_{T,j}(t)}{2\pi}\,d\phi\,dt.$$

Equivalently, these densities define three measures on the same coordinate space $(K,\mathcal B(K))$.

| Model | $T=q_j(U)$ | Inverse $U=q_j^{-1}(T)$ | Density $f_{T,j}(t)$, $0<t<1$ | $P_j(E)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| Uniform endpoints | $\cos\,(\pi U/2)$ | $(2/\pi)\arccos(T)$ | $2/(\pi\sqrt{1-t^2})$ | $1/3$ |
| Uniform radial distance | $U$ | $T$ | $1$ | $1/2$ |
| Uniform midpoint area | $\sqrt U$ | $T^2$ | $2t$ | $1/4$ |

For each row,

$$P_j(E)=\int_0^{1/2}f_{T,j}(t)\,dt=Q\bigl(\Psi_j^{-1}(E)\bigr).$$

There is no equality between $P_A(E)$, $P_B(E)$ and $P_C(E)$ to be contradicted: the measures are different. By contrast, on the common uniform source space $(\Omega_0,\mathcal F_0,Q)$, the measure $Q$ stays fixed while the sampling maps change. The event preimages $\Psi_j^{-1}(E)=\{(u,v):L_j(u,v)>\sqrt3R\}$ are different sets, with $Q$-measures $1/3$, $1/2$, and $1/4$. Within a fixed model, a correct reparametrization preserves event probability.

### A reparametrization within one fixed model

Retain Model B and set $W=T^2$. Since $T$ is uniform on $(0,1)$,

$$P_B(W\le w)=P_B(T\le\sqrt w)=\sqrt w,\qquad f_{W,B}(w)=\frac1{2\sqrt w},\quad0<w<1.$$

The inverse transformation is $T=\sqrt W$. The same event is now $W<1/4$, and

$$P_B(E)=\int_0^{1/4}\frac{dw}{2\sqrt w}=\frac12.$$

If $W$ were instead declared uniform, its density would be changed to 1. That would give Model C and probability $1/4$. This would be a change of probability model, not merely a change of coordinates.

### The distribution of chord length (additional calculation)

For $0\le x\le2R$, put $z=x/(2R)$. Because $L=2R\sqrt{1-T^2}$ is decreasing in $T$,

$$P_j(L\le x)=P_j\bigl(T\ge\sqrt{1-z^2}\bigr).$$

The three chord-length distribution functions are

$$F_{L,A}(x)=\frac2\pi\arcsin(z),\qquad F_{L,B}(x)=1-\sqrt{1-z^2},\qquad F_{L,C}(x)=z^2.$$

They are 0 for $x<0$ and 1 for $x>2R$. Substituting $x=\sqrt3R$ and taking $1-F_{L,j}(x)$ gives $1/3,1/2,1/4$. These continuous laws assign zero probability to the equality at the threshold.

The set-based definitions follow Jagannathan, Chapters 1, 4 and 11. The comparison in common distance and angular coordinates is also developed in [*Urban Operations Research*, §3.3.2](https://web.mit.edu/urban_or_book/www/book/chapter3/3.3.2a.html). The explicit sampling maps and inverse calculations above are provided here in full.

## 4. The induced law is a probability measure

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ be measurable and define $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$. Nonnegativity follows from that of $P$, and

$$P_X(\mathbb R)=P(X^{-1}(\mathbb R))=P(\Omega)=1.$$

If $B_1,B_2,\ldots$ are pairwise disjoint Borel sets, their inverse images are pairwise disjoint events, and inverse images preserve their union. Therefore

$$P_X\!\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}B_n\right)
=P\!\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}X^{-1}(B_n)\right)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(X^{-1}(B_n))
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P_X(B_n).$$

This proves that $P_X$ is a probability measure. The same proof applies to the sampling maps $\Psi_j$ and the induced measures $P_j$ on the chord space. Injectivity is unnecessary for this construction: inverse images exist for all functions.

### Distinct meanings of the notation $f^{-1}$

When $f:\mathsf S\to\mathsf Y$ is a bijection, $f^{-1}(y)$ denotes an element of $\mathsf S$, the value of the inverse function at $y$. For any subset $B\subseteq\mathsf Y$, the notation $f^{-1}(B)$ denotes a subset of $\mathsf S$, the inverse image. The latter is defined even when $f$ is not one-to-one. In the Bertrand construction, $C$ and each $\Psi_j$ are bijections on the stated restricted domains, whereas the chord-length function $L$ is not one-to-one.

## 5. Why ordinary length cannot measure every subset {#vitali-set}

The desired length assignment is more specific than an arbitrary probability measure. It is nonnegative, countably additive, assigns an interval its ordinary length, and is unchanged by translating a measurable set along the real line.

::: {.callout-note title="Scope of the claim"}
The claim is not that no probability measure can exist on the power set of $[0,1]$. A point-mass probability, for example, can be defined on every subset. The obstruction concerns extending ordinary length to every subset while retaining countable additivity and translation invariance.
:::


#### Step 1: group points that differ by a rational number

For $x,y\in[0,1]$, define

$$x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Q.$$

For example, $0.1$ and $0.3$ belong to the same group because their difference is rational. The points $0$ and $\sqrt2/2$ belong to different groups.

This is an equivalence relation: the difference of a point with itself is rational, reversing a rational difference keeps it rational, and adding two rational differences keeps it rational. Its equivalence classes partition $[0,1]$.

#### Step 2: select one representative from each group

Using the **axiom of choice**, choose exactly one point from each equivalence class. Let $V\subseteq[0,1]$ be the set of chosen representatives. Such a selection is called a **Vitali set** here.

This is an existence construction. It does not provide an explicit list of the selected points or a simple interval description. We should not present it as a set that students can enumerate or draw accurately. The argument works for any such choice of representatives.

#### Step 3: examine its rational translates

For every $q\in\mathbb Q\cap[-1,1]$, define

$$V+q=\{v+q:v\in V\},\qquad
W=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q\cap[-1,1]}(V+q).$$

There are countably infinitely many rational shifts in this range. Two facts matter.

**Different translates are disjoint.** If $v_1+q_1=v_2+q_2$, then $v_1-v_2=q_2-q_1$ is rational. Thus $v_1,v_2$ belong to the same equivalence class. Because $V$ chose only one representative from each class, $v_1=v_2$, and then $q_1=q_2$.

**Their union covers the unit interval but stays in a bounded interval.** Every $x\in[0,1]$ has a representative $v\in V$ in its class, and $q=x-v\in\mathbb Q\cap[-1,1]$. Hence $x\in V+q$. Also $0\le v\le1$ and $-1\le q\le1$ imply $-1\le v+q\le2$. Therefore

$$[0,1]\subseteq W\subseteq[-1,2].$$

#### Step 4: suppose ordinary length could measure $V$

This step uses length $\lambda$ on the real line as an auxiliary tool. We are not treating points outside $[0,1]$ as outcomes of the original probability experiment.

If $V$ were Lebesgue measurable, its translates and their countable union would also be measurable. Put $c=\lambda(V)$. Translation invariance gives $\lambda(V+q)=c$ for every shift. Countable additivity and the preceding inclusions would then require

$$1\le\lambda(W)=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q\cap[-1,1]}c\le3.$$

There is no nonnegative value of $c$ satisfying this:

- If $c=0$, the countable sum is zero, contradicting the lower bound 1.
- If $c>0$, the sum is infinite, contradicting the upper bound 3.

Thus $V$ is **not Lebesgue measurable**, and so it is not Borel either. There is no ordinary length $\lambda(V)$ to use as its uniform probability.

The conclusion is about the entire consistent length assignment, including the translated sets and countable unions. It is not a claim that merely writing an arbitrary number next to $V$ immediately contradicts the probability axioms. That number would not by itself supply the usual translation-invariant length model.

#### Interpretation of the construction

For finite $\Omega$, we can assign weights to individual outcomes and add them over every subset. On $[0,1]$, insisting on the standard uniform-length model requires an appropriate measurable event collection. The Borel or Lebesgue sigma-algebra supplies such a collection; the power set is too large for ordinary length.

This distinguishes two different reasons for excluding a set from an event collection. The finite set $\{1,3\}$ is omitted by a parity-only description but can be added without difficulty to the fair-die model. The Vitali set is not assigned a value by Lebesgue length even on its larger, completed sigma-algebra. Not every non-Borel set is non-Lebesgue-measurable: completion adds some non-Borel sets, but it still does not include $V$.

### Exact values, coarse bands and measurability {#coarse-observations}

Use the uniform-length model of Section 1 and the identity random variable $U(u)=u$. Exact observation of $U$ gives

$$\sigma(U)=\mathcal B([0,1]).$$

If the ambient event collection is Borel, this equals $\mathcal F$. If the ambient model uses the completed Lebesgue collection, then $\sigma(U)$ is the Borel subcollection of that larger $\mathcal F$. Generated sigma-algebras are not automatically completed.

Now record only a band:

$$Z(u)=\begin{cases}
0,&0\le u<0.2,\\
1,&0.2\le u<0.7,\\
2,&0.7\le u\le1.
\end{cases}$$

Its three level sets $I_0,I_1,I_2$ are the displayed intervals. The generated sigma-algebra again consists of their eight possible unions. Under uniform length,

$$P(Z=0)=0.2,\qquad P(Z=1)=0.5,\qquad P(Z=2)=0.3.$$

For the overlapping questions $A=\{Z\le1\}$ and $B=\{Z\ge1\}$,

$$P(A)=0.7,\qquad P(B)=0.8,\qquad P(A\cap B)=0.5.$$

The event $[0,0.1]$ is Borel in the full model, but does not belong to $\sigma(Z)$: it splits the first band. Observing $Z=0$ does not determine whether $U\le0.1$. This is an information restriction, not a failure of that interval to possess a length.

There is also a useful limit to the construction. For the Vitali set $V$, the function $H=\mathbf1_V$ still generates the abstract sigma-algebra

$$\sigma(H)=\{\varnothing,V,V^c,[0,1]\}.$$

However, it is **not** a random variable on the Borel or Lebesgue uniform-length model, because its inverse-image event $V$ is not in the ambient event collection. We could give the two groups an arbitrary probability assignment on this four-set collection, but that would not provide the standard uniform-length model on all ordinary intervals together with $V$ and its translates.

### An equivalent construction on the circle {#vitali-circle}

Section 1 uses Borel sets for the continuous model. Why not simply use
every subset, as in the finite audit? Under the axiom of choice, the following
construction shows that a normalized, countably additive, rotation-invariant
probability on a circle cannot be defined on all its subsets.

#### The setting

Let $\Omega=[0,1)$ and define addition modulo $1$,

$$x\oplus y=\begin{cases}x+y,&x+y<1,\\x+y-1,&x+y\ge1,\end{cases}$$

with $\ominus$ the corresponding subtraction. Under $\oplus$ the set $[0,1)$ is an abelian group; identifying $0$ with $1$ makes it a circle, and $x\mapsto x\oplus t$ is a rotation. For $A\subseteq[0,1)$ write $A\oplus t=\{a\oplus t:a\in A\}$.

Suppose $P$ assigns a nonnegative real number to **every** subset of $[0,1)$ and satisfies

1. $P([0,1))=1$;
2. countable additivity;
3. rotation invariance: $P(A\oplus t)=P(A)$ for all $A$ and all $t\in[0,1)$.

#### The construction

Let $\mathbb Q_0=\mathbb Q\cap[0,1)$, a countable subgroup of $([0,1),\oplus)$. Define $x\sim y$ when $x\ominus y\in\mathbb Q_0$. This is an equivalence relation, and its classes are the cosets $x\oplus\mathbb Q_0$.

By the axiom of choice, let $V\subseteq[0,1)$ contain exactly one element of each class.

**Claim 1: the sets $V\oplus q$, for $q\in\mathbb Q_0$, are pairwise disjoint.** Suppose $v_1\oplus q_1=v_2\oplus q_2$ with $v_1,v_2\in V$. Then $v_1\ominus v_2=q_2\ominus q_1\in\mathbb Q_0$, so $v_1\sim v_2$. Since $V$ has one element per class, $v_1=v_2$, and therefore $q_1=q_2$.

**Claim 2: these sets cover $[0,1)$.** Given $x\in[0,1)$, let $v\in V$ be the representative of the class of $x$. Then $q=x\ominus v\in\mathbb Q_0$ and $x=v\oplus q\in V\oplus q$.

So $[0,1)$ is the union of countably many pairwise disjoint sets, each a rotation of $V$.

#### The contradiction

Write $c=P(V)$. Rotation invariance gives $P(V\oplus q)=c$ for every $q$, and countable additivity applied to the countable disjoint family of Claim 1, whose union is $[0,1)$ by Claim 2, gives

$$1=P([0,1))=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q_0}P(V\oplus q)=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q_0}c .$$

Since $P$ is nonnegative, $c\ge0$. If $c=0$ the right-hand side is $0$; if $c>0$ the sum diverges. Neither equals $1$, so no such $P$ exists.

Moreover, if $V$ were Lebesgue measurable, each $V\oplus q$ would be measurable with the same Lebesgue measure: addition modulo 1 is an ordinary translation on each of two pieces. The same countable sum would then contradict the Lebesgue measure of $[0,1)$ being 1. Thus $V$ is not Lebesgue measurable. This is the Vitali construction on the circle.

#### Scope of the conclusion

The contradiction uses both countable additivity and rotation invariance.
Finite additivity alone does not justify the countably infinite sum above.
Removing invariance changes the question: for example, the point mass
$P(A)=\mathbf1_{\{0\in A\}}$ is a countably additive probability on every
subset of $[0,1)$, but it is not rotation invariant.

The selection of $V$ uses the axiom of choice; the argument does not give a
membership rule for $V$. No restriction proved here prevents assigning
probabilities to the Borel events used in this course. Intervals, disks,
angular sectors and the sampling-map preimages in Section 3 are measurable.
The construction explains a boundary of the all-subsets approach; it is not
needed to carry out the practical calculations in the main lesson.

## Advanced: a continuous ticket-closure model

The triplet is often not written out in routine probability calculations. To
see what remains implicit, consider a ticket selected from a specified
service process, and let $T_c$ be its closure time, measured in hours. The
question

> What is the probability that this ticket takes more than one day to close?

is written $P(T_c>24)$, since one day is 24 hours. In an underlying
ticket-system experiment, each outcome $\omega$ determines a closure time
$T_c(\omega)$ in hours. The event of interest is the inverse image

$$T_c^{-1}((24,\infty))=\{\omega\in\Omega:T_c(\omega)>24\}.$$

For an illustrative calculation, suppose the closure time follows a Gamma
distribution with shape $\alpha=2$ and scale $\theta=12$ hours. These are
hypothetical model parameters, not estimates from the six-ticket audit. Under
the shape-scale parameterization, the density is

$$f_{T_c}(t)=\frac{t^{\alpha-1}e^{-t/\theta}}
{\Gamma(\alpha)\theta^\alpha},\qquad t\geq 0.$$

Here $\alpha,\theta>0$ and
$\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty u^{a-1}e^{-u}du$ for $a>0$; in particular,
$\Gamma(2)=1$. With $\alpha=2$ and $\theta=12$ hours, this becomes

$$f_{T_c}(t)=\frac{t}{12^2}e^{-t/12},\qquad t\geq0,$$

where $t$ is measured in hours. Here $\alpha$ is the shape parameter, not the
mean. The mean in this shape-scale parameterization is
$E[T_c]=\alpha\theta=24$ hours. The plotted curve shows this model and shades
the area to the right of the 24-hour cutoff, which coincides with the mean.

![Gamma density for ticket closure time $T_c$ under the illustrative model. The
vertical line marks both the mean and the 24-hour cutoff; the shaded right
tail represents $P(T_c>24\text{ h})$.](../materials/01-probability/gamma-ticket-tail.svg)

For the six-ticket experiment in the main notes, probabilities were calculated by
counting equally likely IDs: $P(C)=|C|/6$. A continuous ticket time cannot
be handled by counting individual possible durations. Under a density model,
the probability of an interval is the area under the density over that
interval. A density value is not itself a probability; integration accumulates
the density across the range. In the audit model, the corresponding finite
calculation is a sum of singleton probabilities; for example,
$P(C)=\sum_{t_i\in C}P(\{t_i\})=4/6$. The closure-time probability is the
integral of its density over the event. With the substitution $u=t/12$,

$$\begin{aligned}
P(T_c>24)
&=\int_{24}^{\infty}\frac{t}{144}e^{-t/12}\,dt\\
&=\int_{2}^{\infty}u e^{-u}\,du\\
&=\left[-(u+1)e^{-u}\right]_2^\infty\\
&=(2+1)e^{-2}=3e^{-2}\approx0.406.
\end{aligned}$$

Thus, under this stipulated model, the probability that closure takes more
than 24 hours is about $0.406$. A different shape, scale or target ticket
population would give a different value. Specifying the Gamma family alone
would not suffice; the parameters and their parameterization are needed.

### What a probability density specifies

The calculation above uses an area, not a density height. Formally, a random
variable $T$ has a **probability density function** $f$ if $f$ is nonnegative
and measurable, $\int_{\mathbb R}f(t)\,dt=1$, and

$$P(T\in D)=\int_D f(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every Borel set }D.$$

Here $f(t)=0$ for $t<0$. The same substitution checks normalization:
$\int_0^\infty (t/144)e^{-t/12}dt=\int_0^\infty ue^{-u}du=1$.
A singleton has zero area, so $P(T_c=24)=0$, while a range can have positive
probability. Not every random variable has a density; the Billing indicator
has a discrete law.

### The triplet for the closure-time model

For this calculation, use the following canonical probability space, which
models closure time alone:

$$(\Omega_c,\mathcal F_c,P_c).$$

In the calculation above, the shorthand $P(T_c>24)$ denotes
$P_c(T_c>24)$ on this space. It is distinct from $P$, the uniform measure
used for selecting one of the six audited ticket IDs.

1. **Sample space:** $\Omega_c=[0,\infty)$, the possible closure durations
   measured in hours.
2. **Event collection:** $\mathcal F_c=\mathcal B([0,\infty))$, the Borel
   subsets of the nonnegative real line: sets obtained by intersecting
   Borel subsets of $\mathbb R$ with $[0,\infty)$.
3. **Probability measure:** for every $E\in\mathcal F_c$,

   $$P_c(E)=\int_E f_{T_c}(t)\,dt,
   \qquad f_{T_c}(t)=\frac{t}{144}e^{-t/12},\quad t\geq0.$$

The density integrates to one, so $P_c(\Omega_c)=1$. Define the random
variable by $T_c:\Omega_c\to[0,\infty)$, $T_c(t)=t$. Thus the event of
closure after 24 hours is

$$T_c^{-1}((24,\infty))=(24,\infty)\in\mathcal F_c,$$

and its probability is

$$P_c(T_c>24)=P_c((24,\infty))
=\int_{24}^{\infty}f_{T_c}(t)\,dt.$$

This is one explicit probability space realizing the assumed Gamma law. A
full ticket-system model could use outcomes that also include ticket type,
priority and other information, with closure time as a function on that
larger space. In routine calculations, $T_c\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\text{shape }2,\text{scale }12\text{ h})$
states the induced law needed for probabilities about closure time without
writing the whole triplet. The distribution of $T_c$ does not by itself
describe every other random quantity in the ticket system.

This is why many engineering and AI calculations work directly with random
variables and their distributions after the probability-space foundation has
been established.

## 6. Exercises on the supplement

1. Verify both $C^{-1}(C(\phi,t))=(\phi,t)$ and $C(C^{-1}(c))=c$ on the stated domains. Explain why the restriction on $t$ is needed.
2. Verify both inverse identities for $q_A(u)=\cos\,(\pi u/2)$ on $(0,1)$. Repeat for $q_C(u)=\sqrt u$.
3. Integrate each density in the comparison table over $(0,1)$ and over $(0,1/2)$.
4. Derive the three chord-length distribution functions from the distance distribution functions.
5. Prove that the inverse image of a union is the union of the inverse images. Use this to explain why the induced law is countably additive.
6. For one roll of a die, decide whether each of the following is a sample space, giving a reason: (a) $\{1,\ldots,6\}$; (b) $\{\text{even},\text{odd}\}$; (c) $\{\text{at most }3,\text{at least }3\}$; (d) $\{\text{less than }3,\text{equal to }3,\text{greater than }3\}$.
7. In the [circle version of the Vitali construction](#vitali-circle), identify the step that fails if $\mathbb Q_0$ is replaced by a finite subgroup of $([0,1),\oplus)$, and state what the argument then yields.
8. Connect the elementary experiments to Models A–C. (a) For Experiment I, find the second endpoint from $a=(1,0)$ and angle $\theta$. Then randomize the first endpoint uniformly, independently of $\theta$, and prove that the two endpoint angles are independent and uniform. Show that the length law is unchanged. (b) Give Experiment II an independent uniform midpoint direction. Explain why its length law is unchanged. (c) Identify the relation between Experiment III and Model C. Finally, compare the probability of containing $a$ in Experiment I and Model A. Does an equal length law imply an equal chord measure?
9. The density $f_{T,A}(t)=2/(\pi\sqrt{1-t^2})$ is unbounded as $t\uparrow1$. Verify that it is integrable and find $P_A(T>1-\varepsilon)$ for $0<\varepsilon<1$. What happens as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$?
10. In Model B, write the event $T<1/3$ in terms of $W=T^2$. Calculate its probability using the distribution function of $W$.

## Further reading on sigma-algebras

James Aspnes, Yale University, [“Martingales,” Section 2: Sigma-algebras](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/pinewiki/Martingales.html), discusses generated sigma-algebras and information retained by observations. The worked LED, response-category and banded-observation examples above illustrate these distinctions. All application records are hypothetical teaching examples.
